title: End-to-end performance engineering for web applications
concepts: Performance is a user-visible property across browser, network, API, database, dependencies, and operations; no single component metric explains the whole journey.
Begin with a user journey, workload, success threshold, and baseline. Define latency percentiles, throughput, error rate, resource use, and cost at explicit boundaries before optimizing.

A request path is a queueing system: concurrency and fan-out amplify tail latency, while retries and unbounded queues can increase load during overload. Budget timeouts and capacity across dependencies.

Browser performance includes resource discovery, caching, critical rendering, JavaScript/main-thread work, React rendering/hydration, and interaction responsiveness; API speed alone is not page speed.

ASP.NET Core performance depends on async I/O, thread-pool health, allocations/GC, serialization, middleware, connection pools, payloads, and downstream waits. Async improves resource use for waits but does not make CPU work faster.

EF Core and SQL Server performance is primarily shaped by query shape, rows/columns transferred, indexes, plans, parameter behavior, locks, round trips, and realistic data; ORM micro-optimizations come after database evidence.
Caching, batching, pagination, streaming, compression, and background work trade freshness, CPU, memory, network bytes, latency, and complexity; each requires correctness and failure policies.

Use traces, metrics, logs, browser profiles, database plans, and runtime profiles together. A profile generates a hypothesis; a controlled experiment tests it and a repeatable measurement confirms the effect.
Capacity and performance are release concerns: load shape, headroom, autoscaling delay, resource limits, canaries, rollback thresholds, and real-user measurements determine whether a change is safe.

practiceProblems.name: Trace and improve a slow checkout journey
practiceProblems.statement: A React checkout has poor p95 completion time despite acceptable API averages. The path includes browser rendering, ASP.NET Core, EF Core, SQL Server, and a payment dependency. Build an evidence-led plan to identify and improve the bottleneck without weakening correctness.
constraints: Do not optimize averages while p95 worsens.
Payment retries can duplicate charges unless the operation is idempotent.
Improving one layer can move the bottleneck elsewhere.

examples.input: p95 4.2 s; browser wait 1.5 s; API span 2.7 s; payment p95 1.8 s; SQL p95 300 ms
examples.output: Trace representative slow requests, split payment and queue wait from app/SQL work, inspect page resource/long-task timing, and set budgets before selecting a change.

practiceProblems.name: Investigate a cross-layer latency regression
practiceProblems.statement: After a deployment, API p99 doubles, browser INP worsens, SQL CPU is unchanged, and the request queue grows. Design a diagnosis and mitigation sequence that considers ASP.NET Core thread-pool behavior, serialization, browser work, dependency timeouts, and rollback.
constraints: A correlation is not sufficient to identify cause.
A retry storm can worsen queue growth.
The mitigation must preserve user data and security.

examples.input: Queue depth rises only for the new release cohort while CPU remains moderate
examples.output: Compare cohort traces, thread-pool queue/blocked work, dependency waits, and payload sizes; mitigate with rollback or traffic reduction while testing a focused hypothesis.

comparisons: Browser user experience metrics versus server request latency: related but measured at different boundaries.
Latency versus throughput: reducing one can increase resource use or reduce sustainable request rate.
Benchmark versus load test versus production measurement: isolated operation cost, system behavior under workload, and real user outcomes answer different questions.
Cache versus source query optimization: cache reduces repeated work but adds freshness, invalidation, memory, and stampede concerns.
Async I/O versus parallelism: async releases blocked threads during waits; parallelism uses concurrent CPU execution and can increase contention.
Profiling versus optimization: profiles identify where to investigate; controlled before/after measurement establishes whether the change helped.

accuracyFacts: Measure percentiles and representative workload; averages can hide tail latency, and coordinated omission can understate latency during pauses.
LCP, INP, and CLS represent different user experience dimensions; server response time does not substitute for these browser metrics.
React Profiler measures React rendering work, not total browser navigation or network time.
Async I/O improves thread utilization during waits but does not make CPU-bound work faster or guarantee unlimited throughput.
EF Core query compilation optimizations do not repair inefficient SQL, poor indexes, excess rows, or avoidable round trips.
A SQL execution plan is an optimizer choice for a particular query and environment; validate with actual workload and runtime evidence.
Retries can amplify load and duplicate side effects; bound retries and require idempotency for safely repeated operations.
Caching trades repeated work for freshness, invalidation, memory, and failure complexity; a cache hit is not inherently correct.
Benchmark, load, stress, spike, soak, capacity, synthetic, and real-user measurements answer different questions.
A before/after improvement must use comparable workload and measurement boundaries; changing workload or cache state invalidates simplistic comparisons.
scopeExclusions: Exhaustive API references for React, .NET diagnostics, EF Core, SQL Server, or browser performance; their specialized topics remain authoritative.
Universal numeric SLO or benchmark thresholds; targets depend on product, workload, device, and business requirements.
Provider-specific load-test, APM, or cloud autoscaling commands beyond the role-level comparison and diagnostic method.
